Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Boeing is asking pilots who fly its 737 jets to pay careful attention to flight instruments after Dutch investigators said a faulty altimeter contributed to the recent crash of a 737 in the Netherlands. Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 broke into three pieces near Schiphol Airport on February 25. The 737 is the most widely flown jet in commercial aviation. More than 6,000 have been sold, according to Boeing. "Boeing reminds all operators to make sure flight crews pay close attention to all primary flight controls during critical stages of a flight," Boeing spokesman Jim Proulx told CNN on Thursday. On February 25, Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 from Istanbul to Amsterdam dropped from the sky on approach to the landing strip at Schiphol Airport, breaking into three pieces in a muddy field. Nine people died and 80 people were hurt in the accident. In a memo to pilots, Boeing says there was a malfunction in one of the plane's two altimeters, which measure the altitude above the terrain where the plane is going to land. The left altimeter was giving "erroneous" information, indicating that the plane was below 7 or 8 feet from ground level when it was actually about 2,000 feet in the air, the memo said. That caused the automatic throttles to slow the plane down. "Boeing recommends operators inform flight crews of the above investigation details and the (Dutch Safety Board) interim report when it is released. In addition, crews should be reminded to carefully monitor primary flight instruments," the memo said. The plane was on automatic pilot when it crashed, said Pieter van Vollenhoven, head of the Dutch Safety Board. The weather was misty at the time of the crash, possibly keeping the pilots from noticing their altitude, Van Vollenhoven said. Automatic pilot should not be used for landings if altimeters are malfunctioning, he said. Dutch investigators said there had been faulty meter readings on two other flights of the same jet, but the pilots were able to land. In the Amsterdam crash, the pilots did not recognize the altimeter problem until it was too late, Van Vollenhoven said. The Boeing memo notes that "the autothrottle, which uses the left radio altimeter data, transitioned to landing flare mode and retarded the throttles to the idle stop. The throttles remained at the idle stop for approximately 100 seconds during which time the airspeed decreased to approximately 40 knots below the selected approach speed." Proulx said he did not know what that speed was for that particular 737 model. The warning issued by Boeing was for many other models of 737 jets, not just the 737-800 involved in the Amsterdam crash.

**Boeing warns 737 pilots after faulty altimeter linked to Amsterdam crash**

Boeing has warned pilots flying its 737 aircraft to closely monitor flight instruments during approach after investigators linked a faulty altimeter reading to the deadly crash of Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 near Amsterdam.

The warning follows findings that one of the aircraft’s radio altimeters — a device that measures the plane’s height above the ground — gave an incorrect reading as the Boeing 737-800 approached Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport. Investigators said the faulty data caused the plane’s autothrottle system to reduce engine power prematurely, contributing to a loss of airspeed before the aircraft crashed short of the runway.

Flight 1951, traveling from Istanbul to Amsterdam, crashed in a field on February 25, 2009. Nine people were killed, including three pilots, and dozens more were injured.

In guidance to airlines, Boeing said pilots should ensure they cross-check altitude and airspeed readings and be prepared to intervene manually if automated systems behave unexpectedly. The company emphasized that flight crews must continue monitoring primary flight instruments, especially during landing approaches when automation is in use.

Dutch investigators have said the radio altimeter on the left side of the aircraft had a history of intermittent problems. During the approach, it reportedly indicated the plane was already near the ground while it was still hundreds of feet in the air. That erroneous reading triggered the autothrottle to enter a landing mode and pull thrust back to idle.

As the aircraft slowed, the crew did not immediately recognize the loss of airspeed, investigators said. The jet stalled and crashed about a mile from the runway.

The crash raised broader concerns about pilot reliance on cockpit automation and the need for crews to respond quickly when automated systems receive faulty sensor data. Aviation safety experts have said modern aircraft systems are highly reliable but can create risks when pilots do not detect incorrect information soon enough.

Boeing said the 737 remains safe when operated according to established procedures and said its warning was intended to reinforce existing training and cockpit monitoring practices.

The Dutch Safety Board’s investigation focused on the interaction between the faulty altimeter, the autothrottle system and crew response during the final minutes of the flight. The board recommended improvements in pilot training, maintenance procedures and aircraft system design to reduce the chances that a single faulty sensor could contribute to a serious accident.

That false low-altitude signal appears to have affected the aircraft’s **autothrottle system**, which responded as though the jet were about to land. The autothrottle reduced engine power to idle, a normal action during the final moments before touchdown, but in this case it occurred far too early.

As a result, the aircraft’s airspeed gradually decreased. Investigators said the crew did not immediately detect the loss of speed. The aircraft eventually approached stall conditions, triggering warnings, but the recovery was not completed in time to prevent impact with the ground short of the runway.

Following the Dutch findings, **Boeing issued a memo to operators of 737 aircraft**, warning crews about the potential effects of erroneous radio-altimeter data on the autothrottle system. The bulletin advised airlines to ensure pilots closely monitor airspeed and altitude during approach, compare radio-altimeter indications, and be prepared to disconnect the autothrottle and manually control thrust if abnormal readings or unexpected power reductions occur.

The Dutch Safety Board emphasized that the findings were preliminary and that the investigation would continue to examine crew actions, training, aircraft systems, maintenance history and operational procedures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the events and investigation surrounding Turkish Airlines Flight 1951, focusing on the faulty radio altimeter, autopilot/autothrottle behavior, casualties, and Boeing’s response to 737 operators.
counterfactuals.output:
Turkish Airlines Flight 1951 was a Boeing 737-800 that crashed on 25 February 2009 while approaching Amsterdam Schiphol Airport from Istanbul. The aircraft came down in a field short of runway 18R during an ILS approach.

The Dutch Safety Board investigation found that a key initiating factor was a faulty left radio altimeter. During the approach it intermittently and then persistently indicated an erroneous height of about minus 8 feet, even though the aircraft was still roughly 1,950 feet above ground. On the 737NG, the autothrottle system used the left radio-altimeter input. Because it believed the aircraft was already at or near touchdown, the autothrottle entered its landing “RETARD” mode and reduced both engines to idle thrust.

The autopilot itself continued to fly the ILS approach, so the aircraft remained broadly on the glide path for a time. However, with the engines at idle, airspeed decayed. The crew did not notice the abnormal autothrottle mode and falling speed in time, partly because of workload, training issues, and expectation that the automation was managing thrust. When the stick shaker activated, the response was delayed and insufficient; thrust was added too late to recover fully. The aircraft stalled and crashed short of the runway.

There were 135 people on board. Nine people were killed, including the three pilots in the cockpit, and more than 80 were injured.

The investigation concluded that the crash resulted from a combination of the radio-altimeter malfunction, the autothrottle’s design logic, the crew’s monitoring and recovery failures, and shortcomings in training and procedures for automation surprises. The Dutch Safety Board also criticized Boeing because previous radio-altimeter/autothrottle events on 737NG aircraft had shown a similar hazard, but operators had not been warned with sufficient urgency or clarity.

After the accident, Boeing issued guidance to 737 operators warning that erroneous radio-altimeter readings could cause unexpected autothrottle retardation during approach. Operators were reminded that crews must closely monitor airspeed, thrust and flight-mode annunciations, and should disconnect the autothrottle and manually set thrust if the system behaves unexpectedly or if radio-altimeter indications are unreliable. Boeing also supported procedural and training changes emphasizing automation monitoring and stall recovery.

**Boeing Warns 737 Pilots After Schiphol Crash Linked to Faulty Altitude Data**

Boeing has issued a warning to airline pilots flying its 737 aircraft after investigators found that an erroneous altitude reading likely played a critical role in the crash of a Boeing 737-800 on approach to Amsterdam Schiphol Airport.

The warning follows the crash of **Turkish Airlines Flight 1951**, a Boeing 737-800 that came down short of the runway while approaching Schiphol. The aircraft broke into several pieces after impacting a field near the airport. Nine people were killed, including members of the flight crew, and dozens more were injured.

Dutch investigators said early evidence pointed to a malfunction in one of the aircraft’s **radio altimeters**, a system that measures the jet’s height above the ground during the final stages of flight. According to the Dutch Safety Board, the left radio altimeter transmitted an incorrect reading indicating that the aircraft was already at or below ground level while it was still hundreds of feet in the air.

That false altitude information was fed into the aircraft’s automated flight systems. Investigators said it caused the **autothrottle system** to reduce engine thrust prematurely, as if the aircraft were landing. With the throttles pulled back, the 737 lost speed during the approach. The crew did not immediately detect the decaying airspeed, and the aircraft entered a stall before crashing short of the runway.

In response, Boeing reminded operators that pilots must closely monitor airspeed and thrust settings during approaches, especially when flying with the autopilot and autothrottle engaged. The company warned that erroneous radio-altimeter data could lead to an unexpected reduction in engine power and urged flight crews to be prepared to disconnect automated systems and manually advance the throttles if needed.

Dutch investigators also noted that the aircraft had experienced **previous radio-altimeter problems** before the fatal flight. Records showed earlier incidents in which the same type of faulty altitude indication had occurred, including events involving abnormal readings from the left radio altimeter. Those prior malfunctions are now a key part of the investigation into why the system’s failure was not corrected before the crash.

The Schiphol accident renewed scrutiny of automation on modern flight decks, particularly the way a single faulty sensor can influence multiple systems during critical phases of flight. While the 737-800 is one of the world’s most widely used aircraft and has a strong safety record, investigators said the crash highlighted the importance of pilot awareness when automated systems behave unexpectedly.

Boeing’s advisory did not ground the aircraft or call for an immediate fleet-wide modification, but it emphasized existing procedures for monitoring radio-altimeter reliability, autothrottle behavior and airspeed. Airlines operating 737s were expected to review the guidance with flight crews and reinforce approach procedures.

The Dutch Safety Board’s final findings later concluded that the faulty altimeter reading, the resulting automatic throttle reduction, and the crew’s delayed response to the loss of airspeed all contributed to the accident. The crash remains one of the most significant examples of how automation, sensor failure and cockpit workload can combine during a routine approach to produce a catastrophic outcome.
